t77a_j00: That’s one grown-up doing three jobs, not three more people moving in to help with the rent, and each job keeps the others in balance. Say a party gets to be too much for your little one. The Protector gets you both out of there, and on the way home the Nurturer tells them they did great, even though mostly they hid in the bathroom. And the Guide helps them think twice about the next weird party they might go to, avoiding another cycle of bathroom vacationing. 🙈
t77a_j01: The Guide is the one people misunderstand the most. I left it out of my first version of this guide until my friend Key pointed it out, and without an inner Guide, it’s easy to go looking for one in a cult. Our lives can become small and like a never-ending therapy session when we focus only on caring for ourselves rather than giving ourselves a mission as well. That’s the Guide’s job. But on the other hand, some people over-rely on their discipline or their mission to avoid caring for themselves.
t77a_j03: Then there are people you’re just getting to know. Meeting them can turn into a kind of test--”First impressions are everything,” as they say, but it could be even worse than that, if you need them to prove you’re lovable. Nobody’s a reassurance machine. I’m giving you permission now to quit school and flunk the tests. Get curious about who this person is, and who you are, and let both of you have your own reasons for being there in the beautiful present. Leaning on each other is still a big part of relationships, and it goes both ways. In a real crisis, getting a safe person involved can be exactly the right move.
t77a_j04: The same goes for doctors. If a hospital held you against your will, or a treatment hurt you, no wonder asking for help feels scary. Bring someone you trust to speak up for you (it doesn’t have to be the relative who never respected your wishes), and ask what a treatment’s for.
t77a_j05: Then there’s the stuff that’s hardest to tell anyone, though it’s often exactly what you need help with. Maybe it’s an urge that scares you, or something you did that could get you in legal trouble. (An urge you’ve never acted on isn’t the same as something you did, by the way.) You know that DM you deleted? It can still be sitting on their phone as a screenshot 🙈, and whatever’s on a company’s server can get handed over if a court asks. A fake name doesn’t guarantee you’re anonymous, either. And some of the people you’d tell, like therapists, teachers, and doctors, can be required to report certain things (a few laws cover everybody, too). Which things depends on where you live, and it’s nowhere near every crime you might mention. The cops are hopefully the obvious ones to be careful with, even if they pretend to care.
t77a_j06: So I’d ask them, before handing over any tricky specifics: “What does the law require you to report?” That's a normal and expected question. Although personally I wouldn't even bother with that. You can always rephrase things as a dream narrative to get the emotional content across without triggering alarm bells (although I actually got in trouble with TalkSpace therapy bot even for a dream!). Just don’t hold back a danger that’s happening now from people who can help, and get anyone in danger safe before worrying about the rest. Sometimes telling on yourself is the thing that keeps someone safe, whatever it costs you legally.
t77a_j07: One practical door anyone can use to slowly experience divine love is gratitude (even after the Turkey’s done & Thanksgiving is over!). Genuinely cultivated gratitude (not just empty/forced ritual) is one way to experience divine love for the first time, or to get it back when the feeling fades. I think it’s essential if we want to live in that love instead of occasionally visiting it.
t77a_j08: This is a bit tricky to put into words, but let me try anyway… You may be suffering now, but you could be suffering more. That’s something to be grateful for. I’m not talking just about changing your “glass half empty” perception to a glass “half full perception.” I’m not pushing “toxic positivity.” Being thankful shouldn’t be pushed on people who just need to grieve for the moment. On the other hand, I’ve noticed that I can sometimes completely flip a bad psychedelic trip into a good one with gratitude alone.
t77a_j09: And I’m certainly not preaching “prosperity philosophy,” even though it can seem to start at that. We still need to remember that if we can only be thankful for the good things we have, we can fall into the trap of thinking that what we have is happiness itself. I’m ultimately reaching for something much deeper.
t77a_j10: Of course, that’s not to say you should not try to suffer less, nor does gratitude for difficulties justify staying with an abuser. The point of life, according to every spiritual tradition and religion, I think, is to suffer less, which first requires us to understand the cause of suffering, and what real suffering and real happiness are. If you, like Biggie Smalls, have come to understand that having money is not real happiness, that’s a big deal! That’s something to be grateful for. Because getting what you want is an endless loop, and it doesn’t lead to being content with less. When you can see that less is more, at a deeper level, that’s where the real gratitude flourishes.
t77a_j11: Sometimes the urge to get away from what’s coming up emotionally gets a lot bigger. All of a sudden you need a drink, or that ex doesn’t seem so bad after all. Some people start a whole new business. If that’s you, it might mean you got close to something that really hurts, and that can be progress, honestly! I’d thank whatever part of you came up with the escape plan, and slow down. If it’s more than you can hold right now, I’d get someone steady with you.
t77a_j12: So why not just blast right past that part, with intensive meditation or psychedelics? Both can get you past the guards before there’s a grown-up big enough to hold whatever comes through, so I’d hold off until there’s enough Nurturer and Protector around. How much is enough depends partly on the medicine and what therapy is done with it.
t77a_j13: Like MDMA, San Pedro is more protective and nurturing than many other medicines, especially at lower doses, so you don’t need as much Nurturer and Protector built up for those, though you still need some. Some people benefit more from solo therapy, while others benefit more from having a trained therapist guide the experience.
t77a_j14: I’d learn to do inner-child therapy sober first, in your ordinary mindstate, since that’s the one you’ll be living in. Cars don’t start at 60mph, that’s not the way the universe seems to work. First gear leads to second leads to third, etc. Second gear, in this case, may refer to gentle meditation or self-hypnosis. When you’re ready, my self-hypnosis guide and lucid-dreaming guide can take those deeper, into third gear. Low doses of entheogens can also synergize compatibly with various gears: cactus, CBD tea with sublingual mapacho, Loveyhuasca, iboga, and so on.
t77a_j15: Remember those guards from The Urge to Escape, above? Same deal here, so get enough Nurturer and Protector in the room before you go deep. Borrowed is fine, as long as it’s from someone steady who won’t try to run your trip for you. And yes, those caution signs still count. But feeling attacked by a demon on a psychedelic is not necessarily paranoia. It can be real, and it’s also not bad unless you’re unprepared. It can be supremely empowering when you can send love and see how it fixes the situation.
t77a_j16: Now, the beautiful stuff. Say one night (on a psychedelic, in a dream, ten days into a meditation retreat, whatever) you felt more love than you knew was possible. Wonderful, and it matters! Keep it as a reference point, and chase it playfully, because it is already a part of you, and you’ll be like a cat chasing its tail, which can be cute and fun, or dizzy and absurd!
t77a_j17: One reason the peak is so momentary is because we often don’t need to truly give anything up to get it. Say you’re still pretty angry, and you want enlightenment, but it has to come with the money and the partner in one package. Ketamine can get you to a peak anyway. Then, you might now have some kind of transcendental “understanding” glimpse that seems like it could fix everything, if only you could be more aware of it, which often leads into a cycle of taking more and more medicine over time. I’d prefer to ask if any of the discontent has been let go, or the anger? If not, that peak was less the love we’re after here than “I’ll be grateful once I’ve got it all,” the gratitude with conditions from Ask God for a Loan.
t77a_j18: And if your little one still can’t take the love in? Hold off on going for bigger, crazier breakthroughs, however tempting it is, or at least know that they are a double-edged sword. Something’s in the way, and getting to know it is your next job. Often it’s a protective part that’s seen love come with strings before. Hear it out first, the way you did in Hear the Protective Part First.
t77a_j19: All kinds of psychoactive drugs can mess with your sense of what’s real, and that’s often the point of them, so you can break free of all your old patterns completely for a bit. But in general, try to select the healthiest ones and use slow and gentle protocols. I’d say one of the most abused psychedelics (aside from ketamine, if you call that a psychedelic) is 5-MeO-DMT. I have a guide on that. People very often believe you need a huge dose of it for a “full release.” They go through all kinds of screaming and shaking, nearly killing themselves, with absolutely zero inner-child work being done. It’s all spiritual bypassing.
t77a_j20: Your own drug history matters too. If you go manic, psychotic (by which I mean losing your sense of reality to the point of posing a risk to yourself or others), get super paranoid, or end up worse afterward than before, those are signs to reconsider trying the same thing again, and try to figure out why that happened. I’d look at the drug and the dosage, as well as mindset and setting etc.
t77a_j21: Paranoia during a rough trip can be a warning sign for psychosis, but it doesn’t automatically lead there, since it can be valid. It tends to go that way when it isn’t balanced by practicality. “The CIA is mind-controlling me!” is paranoia. “The CIA, marketers, and other forces are conspiring to mind-control me, the way they do to everyone else! But since I can see that, I can prevent it to some extent, just by being aware of how it operates” is paranoia too, but it’s practically useful, and less likely to lead to psychosis. “...which means I can prevent it by standing on my head and counting backwards from 33, since 33 is their magic Freemason number!” is leaning psychotic. Some drugs are known for causing paranoia, like THC, so I’d avoid those. If you can’t clearly understand what happened yourself, get someone qualified to help. And if you have an idea of what happened but aren’t sure, ask someone who knows you well.
t77a_j23: When you’re deeply entranced, you can’t freak out: no matter how scary something is, it’s just like, “Oh, this is scary, OK, oh well.” That’s not a good excuse to take crazy doses tho. I went psychotic once on ayahuasca made with pure THH (an alkaloid from the ayahuasca vine) and Mimosa hostilis bark, which has DMT in it. THH alone isn’t hypnotic (trance-like) enough to keep people safe with higher doses of DMT. I was very lucky that my landlord, a Quaker family friend, was super understanding and talked me down gently. Otherwise the cops might have been called, and I could still be in jail, perhaps, since ayahuasca was illegal there at the time, not to mention I had a bunch of mimosa bark in the house that they might have claimed was for distributing. In general, don’t call the cops and expect it to go well. That’s a real last resort.
t77a_j24: Physical pain can bring on the urge to escape too. Say an attack has you curled up on the bathroom floor, and whatever knocked the pain out last time (say, fent, or ketamine) starts looking real good, though you know it’ll leave you worse if you keep resorting to that quick fix.
t77a_j25: By now, you may have already been through a million doctors who shrugged their shoulders, or even alternative treatments that were too costly or hard to grade. Sometimes it really is so simple that the best doctors and scanners can’t figure it out, like your house is moldy. It is worth going through all the basic checks first that you can do yourself, and trying the things that make most sense. For more on that, check my detox guide.
t77a_j26: And when the symptoms come and go randomly, the best time to get diagnostics done could be right at the actual time of the crisis, rather than waiting until you feel well enough to make an appointment. But what if the attacks come almost every day? You can’t move into the ER. And normal test results don’t prove the pain is imaginary, just as a treatment that helps doesn’t explain what’s causing it.
t77a_j28: Sometimes, a physical illness is really partly or wholly an emotional issue causing “somatic symptoms,” as happened to various friends of mine, as well as to Lucia Capacchione, PhD., and many of her clients and friends. She wrote one of the first comprehensive inner child therapy guides, Recovery of Your Inner Child, in 1991. While I don’t doubt that many people do recover from mysterious physical illness via meditation, inner child therapy, and somatic therapy, I also don’t want to claim, as some folks do, that all illness is entirely rooted in emotional issues. That is clearly not true. We don’t need to be gaslit to consider all the possibilities.
t77a_j30: After all, sometimes “I want it NOW!” is just that: a rung on the desire treadmill. No hidden protector or old trauma required, because all creatures have endless desires naturally anyway, especially when immature. You can hear that want without shame about it. Hearing it doesn’t require giving into it, especially if getting your way would hurt you or somebody else.
t77a_j31: Maybe you’d rather that your support person were a lover, as well. Lots of people open a dating app in the middle of the night, hoping someone will make it all stop hurting. 🙈 If that’s you right now, dating can wait while your friends and the steady people around you do their part. That doesn’t mean you have to be completely healed before you date, but romance should follow when two people really love each other and want to build a life together. It won’t rescue you from the pain or reward you for healing, and it sucks to mess up a beautiful relationship because of unhealed trauma, believe me, I know. I wrote a whole romance guide, mostly due to this.
